# Notes on Genesis 5 for a verse-by-verse commentary

**What I couldn't find:** My searches didn't turn up any NET Bible notes, any Bible Odyssey article, or any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter, so none of those appear below. For the Lutheran view I only found one Luther quotation, and it comes second-hand through Enduring Word. Some Bible Hub "q" pages show up below. These are unsigned question-and-answer pages that argue a young-earth position, so they are weaker sources than the named commentators.

---

**Chapter overview**
- Benson says the list covers only the "holy seed" from whom Christ came, not all of Adam's descendants. These were the people who kept the promise after the first Adam and were the ancestors of the second Adam, at whose coming the promise was fulfilled. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/5-1.htm
- Ray Pritchard (quoted on Precept Austin) calls these ten men who lived by faith at a time of growing unbelief and widespread secularism. https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-5-commentary
- Constable: Lamech is sixth in Cain's list (Genesis 4) and Enoch is sixth in Seth's list. He takes this as God pointing out the contrast between the two lines: one ungodly, one godly. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/5-5.html
- Coffman rejects the opposite idea. He says it is wrong to treat this list as just another version of Cain's line; the similar names mean nothing and are common in Hebrew genealogies. He also rejects linking the chapter to "P," the supposed priestly source. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/genesis-5.html

**Where Protestants really differ: are there gaps in the list, and how old is the earth?**
- *Complete list:* Constable says recording each father's age when his son was born strongly suggests the list is complete. The lists in 1 Chronicles 1:1-4 and Luke 3:36-38 match it, so there are probably no missing generations. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-5.html
- *Baptist (John MacArthur):* He admits that Princeton scholars William Green and B. B. Warfield, both inerrantists, proposed gaps. But he quotes the view that even the most generous gaps could add only several hundred, or at most about 1,000, years to Ussher's dates. https://www.gty.org/sermons/90-211/the-how-why-and-when-of-creation-part-1,
- *Reformed/Baptist (Desiring God):* This article argues it is doubtful God meant these lists to let us calculate the date of creation. On that reading, "Seth fathered Enosh" could mean Enosh was a descendant many generations after Seth. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/our-old-earth
- *The Gospel Coalition:* Joe Carter summarises Green's case. Shortening and leaving out names is common in biblical genealogies, and no biblical writer ever adds these numbers up. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/debatable-genesis-genealogies-and-the-age-of-the-earth/
- *Middle view (Geisler, quoted on Precept Austin):* Luke 3:36 includes a Cainan whom Genesis leaves out. Geisler concludes it is better to see Genesis 5 and 10 as adequate genealogies, not complete chronologies. https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-5-commentary
- *Enduring Word (David Guzik):* He says biblical genealogies sometimes skip generations. Even allowing for gaps, he finds it hard to put Adam much more than about 10,000 years before Jesus. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-5/

---

**v. 1**
- Clarke: the Hebrew word for "book" can mean any register or written account. Moses repeats the "likeness of God" here to remind people how high humanity fell, and to show that death came from sin rather than from how we were made. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/genesis-5.html
- Guzik: this may be where Adam's own written record ends, passed down to Moses, who edited it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-5/
- Precept Austin: humans were created by God, not evolved. It also notes the contrast between the "book" of Adam here and the "book" of Jesus Christ in Matthew 1:1: one is a record of death, the other of life. https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-5-commentary

**v. 2**
- Bible Hub (Pulpit-style note): verses 1–2 sum up the creation of man. This new section deals only with the generations of man, so it starts from the sixth day. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/5-1.htm
- Guzik: God himself named the race "Mankind," so using the word for the whole human race is not sexist. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-5/

**v. 3**
- *Methodist (Adam Clarke):* The "likeness" here is not the image Adam was created with. Adam had lost his moral likeness to God, so Seth was born imperfect, mortal and sinful like his father. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/genesis-5.html
- Guzik agrees. Everyone except Jesus is born in Adam's fallen image. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-5/
- Bible Hub Q&A puts it differently. It says the verse shows the image of God continuing despite the Fall. https://biblehub.com/q/Genesis_5_6_in_Adam_s_genealogy.htm
- Clarke also explains the numbers. The Hebrew, Samaritan and Greek (Septuagint) texts give different ages, so the total from creation to the Flood is 1,656, 1,307 or 2,242 years depending on the text. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/genesis-5.html

**v. 4**
- Guzik: Adam had many other children who aren't named, and these daughters became the wives of his sons. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-5/
- Matthew Henry: every patriarch except Noah was born before Adam died. They could hear about creation, the fall and the promise from Adam himself. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_005.cfm

**v. 5**
- Barnes: verses 3–5 set the pattern for every entry. Each gives the father's age when a son was born, the years he lived afterwards having sons and daughters, and his death. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/5-5.html
- Clarke: Adam was the first person to die a natural death. Abel's death was violent. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/genesis-5.html
- Gill: these are real solar years, not lunar ones. Otherwise some fathers, such as Enoch, would have had children at an impossible age. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/5-5.html
- Why did they live so long? Guzik believes they really did. The effects of the fall had not yet built up, and the world before the Flood was very different. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-5/
- Bob Utley (bible.org) lists the main views: the ages are figurative, years were counted differently, sin had not yet spread as far, or the large numbers honoured earlier leaders, as in the Sumerian lists of ten ancient kings. https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-5
- *Modern comparison (Holman Bible Dictionary):* The Sumerian kings were treated as gods and said to live tens of thousands of years. The people in Genesis are clearly human, and Genesis stresses the gap between the one God and the people he created. https://www.studylight.org/dictionaries/eng/hbd/a/antediluvians.html

**vv. 6–8 (Seth)**
- Bible Hub Q&A: verse 6 brings in the third name, Enosh, tying him to Adam through Seth. https://biblehub.com/q/Genesis_5_6_in_Adam_s_genealogy.htm
- Guzik: if there are no gaps, Seth died only 14 years before Noah was born. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-5/

**vv. 9–14 (Enosh, Kenan)**
- MacArthur: the repeated "and he died" after each name shows the effect of the fall. https://www.gty.org/sermons/80-387/enoch-walked-with-god
- Spurgeon (quoted by Guzik) tells of a listener whom that refrain woke up to his own mortality and led to Christ. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-5/

**vv. 15–17 (Mahalalel)**
- Precept Austin: his name means something like "praise of God," and he is fourth in descent from Adam in Seth's line. https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-5-commentary

**vv. 18–20 (Jared)**
- Guzik groups Jared with Enoch and Methuselah. He doesn't comment on Jared separately. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-5/

**v. 21**
- Barnes: here "God" appears with the definite article for the first time (literally "the God"). Walking with "the God" hints that others were walking without him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/5-21.htm
- Fausset: Enoch is first said to walk with God only after Methuselah was born. God's gift of children woke a new love for God in him and a deeper sense of responsibility. https://www.studylight.org/dictionaries/eng/fbd/e/enoch.html

**v. 22**
- Guzik: Methuselah's name means "when he is dead, it shall come." He believes Enoch was given a warning of coming judgment, which drew him closer to God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-5/
- *Baptist (Spurgeon):* The walk was continuous and kept moving forward, "not a run, a rush, a leap, a spurt, but a steady walk." Enoch did this while raising a family. https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/enoch
- Barnes: this great saint did not withdraw from family life or ordinary duties. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/5-21.htm
- **A real difference within the Methodist tradition: can a believer live without sinning?**
  - *Adam Clarke (Wesleyan):* The Hebrew verb form shows Enoch was determined to walk with God. Hebrews 11:5 shows that it was possible then to live without sinning against God. If it was possible then, Clarke says, it is surely possible now through the same grace. He also argues marriage does not stand in the way of "the perfection of piety." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/genesis-5.html
  - *George Whitefield (Calvinist Methodist):* He describes Enoch's fellowship with God as holy, settled and habitual, though "undoubtedly not altogether uninterrupted," and enjoyed through Christ Jesus. https://ccel.org/ccel/whitefield/sermons/sermons.iv.html

**v. 23**
- Clarke: Enoch, probably the best of these men, spent the shortest time on earth. His 365 years match the days of a solar year. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/genesis-5.html
- The Pulpit Commentary (quoting Kalisch) rejects reading this as star-based or astrological symbolism. It says the years refer to real individual lives. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/5-21.htm

**v. 24**
- Gill: "walked with God" is repeated to stress it and to show how unusual it was in that corrupt age. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/reb/genesis/5-24.html
- The Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) renders the phrase "pleased God," which is the wording Hebrews 11 uses. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/5-21.htm
- Guzik: walking with God means walking by faith, walking in the light, and walking in agreement with him. Spurgeon wondered whether the other patriarchs actually watched Enoch being taken up. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-5/
- MacArthur: in a sense, Enoch recovers what Adam and Eve lost. He calls Enoch the first preacher of judgment, who had "a private rapture." https://www.gty.org/sermons/80-387/enoch-walked-with-god
- Fausset: Enoch pictures the living believers who will be changed when Christ comes (1 Corinthians 15:51-52). https://www.studylight.org/dictionaries/eng/fbd/e/enoch.html
- *Early church:* Irenaeus said Enoch was taken up in the same body in which he pleased God, pointing ahead to the taking up of the righteous. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0103505.htm
- *Orthodox (OCA):* There is little agreement about who the two witnesses of Revelation 11 are. Seeing them as Elijah and Enoch seems to be the common opinion of many Church Fathers. https://www.oca.org/questions/scripture/two-witnesses-rev-111-14
- *Catholic Encyclopedia:* It says of Elijah, "Like Enoch, he was 'translated', so that he should not taste death." https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/05381b.htm
- *Evangelical (GotQuestions):* It lists three main views of the two witnesses: Moses and Elijah, Enoch and Elijah, or two unknown believers. https://www.gotquestions.org/two-witnesses.html

**vv. 25–27 (Methuselah)**
- Clarke: Methuselah lived until the very year of the Flood, and his name may have been a prophetic warning. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/genesis-5.html
- MacArthur: God let him live longer than anybody else as an act of grace in the face of judgment, and when he died the flood came. https://www.gty.org/sermons/80-387/enoch-walked-with-god
- Clarke on v. 27: even of a man who lived 969 years, Scripture says "he died." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/genesis-5.html

**vv. 28–29 (Noah's name)**
- Clarke: some link "Noah" to a word meaning "comfort," but he thinks it more likely comes from a word meaning "rest." He takes Lamech's words as prophetic, fulfilled when God smelled the "soothing" (literally "rest") aroma of Noah's sacrifice and promised not to curse the ground again (Genesis 8:21). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/genesis-5.html

**vv. 30–31 (Lamech)**
- Guzik: the main point of the chapter is that every one of these men died. Some were great men, but none was the promised deliverer. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-5/
- *Lutheran:* Luther (quoted via Boice in Enduring Word) called these patriarchs, after Christ and John the Baptist, the greatest heroes the world has produced. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-5/

**v. 32**
- Clarke: Japheth was the eldest son, but Shem is named first because the Messiah came from his line. He finds it hard to explain why Ham is not listed in his proper place. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/genesis-5.html
- Constable: Noah's sons are not listed in birth order (compare Genesis 9:24). He also notes that Genesis 11:10-26 has a matching ten-generation list running from Shem to Abraham. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-5.html
